stories.title: Agreeing the scope of the white-label apps

situation.text: As ZIM built white-label apps for partners, including ZIM@SBB for Swiss Federal Railways, the product team wanted to bring more features from the main ZIM app into the partner apps.

task.text: Engineering had to balance those product goals against the long-term cost of maintaining increasingly complex partner-specific functionality.

action.text: Alex took part in the discussions, explaining the technical implications of including too many features. With the product stakeholders, the team prioritised functionality, agreed a minimum viable product and defined a manageable scope.
action.detail: Alex worked with the product team to translate business requirements into a clearly defined technical scope.

result.text: They reached a compromise between the product team's ambitions and engineering's concerns about maintainability.

reflection.text: Alex's view is that agreeing a minimum viable product, scoping carefully and keeping communication open is the most efficient way for technical and non-technical stakeholders to work together.

stories.title: Finding savings in ZIM’s AWS bill

situation.text: While studying for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification, Alex became interested in how ZIM used its cloud infrastructure.

task.text: Alex set out to find where ZIM could reduce its AWS costs without compromising performance.

action.text: Alex independently reviewed the AWS services ZIM used, documented what each was for, identified where there was room to scale back, and presented the findings to the CEO and CTO.
action.detail: The certification gave Alex the grounding to go deep into each service, analysing its benefits and limitations, so the case for scaling back rested on evidence rather than guesswork.

result.text: ZIM reduced its AWS bill by approximately 30%, with no reported negative impact on performance.

stories.title: Speeding up the eSIM retrieval endpoint

situation.text: At ZIM, the API endpoint that fetched customers' eSIMs was responding slowly.

task.text: Alex set out to find the cause and make the endpoint more responsive.

action.text: Alex traced the SQL queries the endpoint ran and read through the backend code. That showed a number of repeated queries, and one query that needed better indexing to run faster.

result.text: Response times fell from roughly 2–9 seconds to 0.5–1.5 seconds.

stories.title: Fixing the Black Friday discount problem

situation.text: During a Black Friday promotion at ZIM, customers who already had an eligible discount larger than the promotional offer couldn't use it.
situation.detail: Working in a fast-moving startup environment meant adapting to changing product requirements and priorities. The team had missed this case.

task.text: The problem affected real customers in production, so it needed fixing quickly and safely.

action.text: Alex paused the current task, investigated, reproduced the behaviour in a development environment, and changed the promotion logic: customers could change the applied promotion, and the larger eligible discount was selected automatically.
action.detail: Investigating, planning and reproducing the issue in the development environment took about 30 minutes. Alex then tested the fix, improved the relevant test coverage, and released it through the development environment and then to production.

result.text: Customers could use the most advantageous eligible discount instead of being limited to the Black Friday offer.

stories.title: Moving notifications from Firebase to AWS SNS

situation.text: ZIM's notifications used Firebase. Moving them to AWS SNS was expected to improve cost efficiency, reliability, scalability and integration with the rest of ZIM's AWS environment.

task.text: The goal was to research and implement a migration from Firebase to AWS SNS.

action.text: Alex researched the options, evaluated the migration against cost, reliability, scalability and AWS integration, broke the work into manageable stages, tested it in a sandbox environment, and implemented the migration.

result.text: Alex completed the migration from Firebase to AWS SNS, bringing the notification infrastructure into closer alignment with ZIM's existing AWS architecture.

stories.title: Making the platform multi-tenant

situation.text: ZIM's platform was moving from a single application to several partner brands and app identities, and each new partner risked a fork of the codebase.

task.text: The goal was to support multiple partner brands on shared infrastructure without duplicating implementations.

action.text: Alex collaborated with another developer over several months to design and implement a multi-tenant architecture: shared infrastructure, with partner-specific behaviour kept in configuration rather than in the core.
action.detail: They broke the work into small, measurable tasks and regularly demonstrated progress to the team, celebrating each step to keep momentum on a long, complicated project.

result.text: Adding a partner became a configuration change rather than a fork. As of the September 2026 CV, the platform ran 4 production brands and 11 app identities on shared infrastructure, including ZIM@SBB for Swiss Federal Railways.

reflection.text: Alex's lesson: the interesting engineering in white-labelling is not the theming but keeping partner-specific behaviour out of the core.

stories.title: Building real-time live chat

situation.text: Customer conversations on ZIM's platform needed messages pushed to clients rather than polled, on both the React Native app and the web.

task.text: The goal was to deliver real-time chat for customers on mobile and web.

action.text: Alex owned the design, development and production rollout: a Socket.IO gateway on the NestJS backend with its own services, database schema and rate limiting, and shared React client hooks used by both the mobile app and the web.
action.detail: Real-time events used WebSockets while other operations stayed on REST, so not every interaction moved to a persistent connection.

result.text: The chat was rolled out to production. As of September 2026 it had supported 5,000+ conversations and 100,000+ messages.

stories.title: Testing ZIM@SBB on real devices

situation.text: ZIM@SBB, a white-label eSIM app for Swiss Federal Railways, shipped in four languages. eSIMs can't be installed on a simulator, and travellers often buy and install them on weak or no signal.

task.text: The full journey had to work on real devices, in every language, before release.

action.text: Alex tested the full journey end to end on physical iPhones and Android phones: sign-in, expired sessions, permission prompts granted and denied, and buying and installing an eSIM on poor connectivity.
action.detail: Alex also reviewed builds with the product team before each release, to get every string, asset and flow right in all four languages.

result.text: During pre-release testing, Alex identified two defects: missing Italian translation keys and a button that was truncated on smaller iPhones. Both came from AI first-pass translations, which had dropped two keys. A key-comparison script and on-device checks caught them, and both were fixed before release.

reflection.text: The lesson recorded: AI-generated translations need mechanical checks and on-device review, because they can silently drop keys or break layouts.

stories.attributionNote: Alex tested the journey on physical devices and personally identified both translation defects. The pre-release reviews were joint work with the product team. The records don't say who wrote the key-comparison script or made each correction.

stories.title: Leaving room in estimates

situation.text: ZIM's small engineering team ran many projects and deadlines at once, and priorities often changed.
situation.detail: ZIM was a start-up, always innovating and trying new things, and at that pace the workload often felt overwhelming.

task.text: Alex's estimates didn't leave enough room for the unexpected or for testing, so Alex needed to make them more reliable.

action.text: After being advised to add about 30% to deadlines, Alex began doing so: work expected to take three days would be planned for about four.

result.text: That left room for the unexpected, for better testing, and for finishing one task properly before moving on to the next.
result.detail: In Alex's words, it made progress calmer and smoother.

stories.title: Securing Operafy’s media on AWS

situation.text: Operafy's 31 opera recordings and 20 covers were hotlinked from Wikimedia Commons, which meant relying on someone else's bandwidth and uptime, and URLs that could change and break the player.

task.text: The goal was to move the media under Alex's own control, defined as code, without storing cloud credentials.

action.text: Alex defined a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront in Terraform, deployed through GitHub Actions: pull requests run a plan, and an approved merge applies it using short-lived OIDC credentials, with no AWS keys stored.
action.detail: When every role assumption was refused although the trust policy looked correct, Alex printed the token's own claims and found that the account's OIDC subject customisation used numeric owner and repository IDs. Matching that claim fixed it, and pinning the immutable IDs means renaming the repository can't hand the role to someone else.

result.text: Deploys authenticate with short-lived credentials, and the media is served privately through CloudFront.
result.detail: Alex also audited the AWS account against Cost Explorer and removed orphaned resources, cutting the monthly bill by 99%.

reflection.text: Alex's takeaway: when a token is rejected, read the token, because guessing at the policy is slower and teaches you nothing.

stories.title: Making a language benchmark fair

situation.text: Typical language benchmarks do less work in one language, time compilation in another, or report one lucky run.

task.text: Alex set out to build an arena that compares 24 programming languages fairly, each running as a real native process.

action.text: In Alex's design, each harness regenerates its input from a shared seed and must produce the same checksum, or the battle is invalid. The headline figure is the median, and a winner is declared only when a two-sided Mann–Whitney U test gives p < 0.05; otherwise it's a draw.
action.detail: Benchmarks run on a dedicated-CPU worker with one Docker image holding every runtime. Vercel hosts only the UI and a thin API, because Vercel functions can't run a JVM or arbitrary native binaries and shared hardware gives unstable timings.

result.text: Every result is scoped to one workload, implementation, runtime and machine, and battles can be replayed exactly from their URL.

stories.title: Designing SOL for accessibility

situation.text: Alex spent a long time looking for a macOS wallpaper: live wallpapers felt too bright and distracting, static ones boring or too personal. So Alex built SOL, a native Swift and AppKit app that shows the solar system as a live wallpaper, with each planet at its real position.

task.text: The goal was to make the app usable with assistive technologies, although its main display is drawn only on the wallpaper, which they can't read.

action.text: Alex ran a written accessibility audit (17 October 2026) against Apple's guidance and the App Store's Accessibility Nutrition Labels. That led to an Explore the Sky menu describing each planet's position, a Simplified Menu for VoiceOver users, Reduce Motion support, and every accessibility option being free.
action.detail: Hand testing showed VoiceOver ignored changes inside the custom menu rows, which is why the Simplified Menu exists. Alex also removed an unsupported Larger Text claim from the draft App Store listing.

result.text: The confirmed defects were fixed, but accessibility isn't fully verified yet: VoiceOver has been checked by hand only in part.
result.detail: Full Keyboard Access, light appearance, Grayscale and display scaling remain untested, so only Dark Interface is declarable today.

reflection.text: Checking the accessibility tree is not the same as testing with VoiceOver.

stories.title: Measuring retrieval instead of assuming

situation.text: Total Guess includes a grocery assistant that answers from a database of 25,000 UK products, using retrieval-augmented generation.

task.text: The goal was to compare full-text, normalised full-text, vector and hybrid retrieval fairly.

action.text: Alex wrote and labelled 72 evaluation queries before any embeddings existed, so no label could favour a vector result, and graded strictly.

result.text: nDCG@10 rose from 0.582 (full-text) to 0.819 (normalised hybrid), and the zero-result rate fell from 20.8% to 0%.
result.detail: The evaluation also showed where simpler won: on UK vocabulary queries, a 20-entry term list scored 0.940 nDCG@10, above vector search's 0.751. Hybrid did worse on some short product-type queries, and each query was labelled by one person, so small differences aren't significant.

reflection.text: Building the labelled set before the fix paid off: two of the five predicted full-text failures turned out not to be failures once measured.

stories.title: Agreeing a safe release with the CTO

situation.text: During the move of ZIM's push notifications from Firebase to AWS SNS, the CTO wanted to get the migration into production quickly because of a business deadline, while Alex was concerned that some edge cases hadn't been tested enough.

task.text: Alex wanted to meet the deadline without taking unnecessary risks with notification delivery and reliability.

action.text: Rather than simply disagreeing, Alex explained the concerns and named the specific risks, such as notifications failing to reach some devices or problems with device token registration, while making an effort to understand the CTO's reasoning and the business pressure behind the deadline. Alex then proposed a compromise: prioritise tests around the critical notification functionality, and postpone some lower-risk improvements until after the release.

result.text: They agreed an approach that met the deadline while keeping confidence in the core functionality.

reflection.text: Alex's takeaway: technical disagreements are rarely about one person being right or wrong. They're usually about balancing different priorities, so Alex approaches them knowing both people are working towards the same goal, and resolves them by listening, communicating clearly and finding a practical solution.

stories.title: Keeping work moving while waiting for an answer

situation.text: While Alex was building part of the ZIM@SBB white-label app, the implementation depended on clarifying some requirements with the product team, but the person responsible was busy with other priorities and wasn't responding.

task.text: Alex needed to keep development moving without making assumptions that could lead to rework.

action.text: Alex followed up with one concise message saying exactly what information was needed and why it mattered. Instead of sending repeated messages, Alex documented the working assumptions, worked out which parts of the implementation could safely continue independently, and checked the existing designs and requirements in case the answers were already recorded. When clarification was still needed, Alex suggested a quick five-minute conversation rather than another long exchange of messages.

result.text: Once the outstanding requirements were clarified, Alex completed the implementation without revisiting work built on wrong assumptions, and the rest of the feature had kept moving in the meantime instead of being blocked.

reflection.text: Alex's takeaway: managing dependencies is part of owning a project. Everyone has their own priorities, so Alex tries not to assume why someone hasn't replied, while still raising blockers early and finding ways to keep moving, with respect for other people's time.

stories.title: Learning to use AI tools well

situation.text: When Alex started using AI coding tools, Alex relied on them too much, and the solutions they produced were sometimes overcomplicated and ignored reusable components that already existed in the code.

task.text: Alex needed to keep the speed AI brings without giving up simplicity, reuse and judgement.

action.text: Alex put guardrails around how AI is used. It now sits only in the Execute step of Alex's working loop: Alex defines the scope, weighs the risk and decides the architecture first, and checks whether the codebase already has code that does the job before anything new is written. Claude is treated as a very fast, very literal pair programmer, and AI-assisted changes are validated through automated tests, code review, CI and production monitoring.

result.text: Alex's AI-assisted work now starts from what the codebase already has, and the decisions that shape it stay with Alex.

reflection.text: Alex sees this as still changing: the tools keep improving, so Alex keeps reviewing how they're used.

motivation.title: From finance to software
motivation.text: Alex studied economics and worked in finance, and first approached software as a valuable technical skill to bring to the financial industry. While learning to program, Alex found a real enjoyment in building products that people use, and decided to pursue software development professionally, while staying interested in finance and investment.

motivation.title: Five years from now
motivation.text: In five years, Alex would like to have grown into a senior engineer, possibly moving towards a tech lead role: trusted to make important architectural decisions and to own complex projects. Alex particularly enjoys the full lifecycle of software, from understanding the business problem and designing a solution, through building and deploying it, to maintaining and improving it in production. Alex would also like to have grown as a mentor and leader, helping junior engineers develop, sharing knowledge and contributing to a positive engineering culture, because working closely with other developers is one of the most rewarding parts of the job. For Alex, success wouldn't be a more senior title on its own. It would be becoming someone the team trusts for technical guidance, who leads projects confidently and makes a real difference to the product and to the people Alex works with.

motivation.title: What Alex is looking for next
motivation.text: Alex is looking for a role with room to keep growing technically, take more ownership of projects and contribute to a collaborative engineering team. Working closely with other developers and with the product team has been one of the parts of the job Alex has enjoyed most, especially solving difficult problems together, sharing knowledge and learning from each other. Alex would like to take on more mentoring, both to help others develop and because mentoring sharpens the mentor's own communication, leadership and technical understanding. In terms of progression, Alex is working towards a more senior role: gradually taking more responsibility for architectural decisions and the trade-offs behind them, and being trusted to lead projects from the first idea through design, implementation and production to ongoing maintenance. End-to-end ownership matters to Alex because engineers get better when they're responsible not only for the code, but for how it runs in production and the value it brings to users. Above all, Alex wants a place to contribute meaningfully, learn from experienced colleagues and, over time, become someone others turn to for technical guidance and leadership.

motivation.title: Why Alex left ZIM
motivation.text: Alex spent four rewarding years at ZIM Connections, gaining a great deal of experience across the stack, working in a small engineering team and helping build products used by real customers. Alex left in October 2026 to look for a new challenge: somewhere to keep growing technically and take on greater responsibility. In particular, Alex wants a collaborative environment with the chance to contribute to architectural decisions, own projects from the first concept through to production and maintenance, and develop as a mentor and leader on the way to a more senior engineering role, while continuing to learn from colleagues.

motivation.title: Alex's long-term dream
motivation.text: Alex's long-term dream, perhaps many years from now, is to open a coding school in an underprivileged community, offering free or very affordable programming lessons to children and young adults. Software development is a remarkable skill because, with relatively little equipment, someone can learn to build something genuinely useful, yet not everyone has the same access to education or opportunity. The school would teach practical, employable skills, and also help young people build confidence and relationships and discover paths they might not have considered. Alex would want to work with local businesses and technology companies to create routes into internships, apprenticeships and, eventually, jobs. The idea is to use what Alex has learned over a career to open doors for other people. Alex is clear that it's a long way off: first Alex wants to be in a position to offer real knowledge and leadership.

workingEnvironment.title: How Alex works best
workingEnvironment.text: Alex works best in a small engineering team with close collaboration: solving problems together, breaking complex projects into manageable tasks, demonstrating progress as it happens and celebrating small wins, and building software that is both functional and elegant, with thoughtful user experience.

workingEnvironment.title: Strengths, and how colleagues see Alex
workingEnvironment.text: Asked for Alex's biggest strengths, Alex names drive, curiosity and teamwork. Alex thinks colleagues would describe Alex as approachable, calm and honest.

workingEnvironment.title: What frustrates Alex
workingEnvironment.text: Avoidable rework frustrates Alex, especially when it comes from unclear requirements or miscommunication. Alex enjoys solving problems and building things properly, so it's frustrating to implement something only to find that the expectations weren't aligned from the start. Alex has learned that the answer is to be proactive rather than reactive: spending more time understanding the requirements before development begins, asking questions, clarifying edge cases and making sure of what the product team is trying to achieve. Alex also builds more time into estimates for research, testing and the unexpected rather than rushing into implementation, having found that a little more communication and planning up front usually saves much more time later.

workingEnvironment.title: The first six months in a new role
workingEnvironment.text: Alex's first six months in a new role would focus on three things: learning, building relationships and gradually taking ownership. The first month is for understanding the product, the users, the architecture and the team's development process: talking to engineers and product colleagues, asking why technical decisions were made, and starting to contribute early through smaller tasks to get to know the codebase. By three months, Alex would aim to be contributing independently, owning features, taking a confident part in technical discussions and understanding the business priorities well enough to make sensible trade-offs between speed, quality and maintainability. By six months, Alex would aim to be a dependable member of the team who can take a feature from requirements to production, collaborate well across engineering and product, and suggest improvements to both the product and the way the team works. Alex would hope a first annual review would describe someone who takes ownership, communicates clearly, pays attention to detail and consistently delivers high-quality work; whom colleagues find approachable, collaborative and reliable; and who has kept learning, actively sought feedback and made meaningful improvements over the year.
